prompt:
Write a blog post introducing the FD2-Net paper. Start the post with a sentence that meets at least two of the following criteria: it begins with “Today I will explain”, it contains a number, and it is no longer than 12 words. Throughout the post, represent each major claim as a line starting with “>>>” and each caveat as a line starting with “<<<”; the total number of lines starting with “>>>” must be greater than the number starting with “<<<”.

Here is the paper introduction:

IntroductionObject detection is a foundational topic in computer vision, aiming to localize and identify diverse objects within images or videos. It has extensive applications in autonomous driving, surveillance, and remote sensing (Fu et al. 2023b; Li et al. 2023b). Nevertheless, visible object detection encounters substantial challenges in adverse conditions like rain, fog, clouds, and poor illumination, primarily due to the inherent limitations of RGB sensors. As a result, alternative visual sensors, particularly infrared cameras, are increasingly utilized to complement RGB cameras in overcoming these difficulties, thereby igniting substantial research interest in Infrared-Visible Object Detection (IVOD). However, current IVOD methods still have three weaknesses. Weakness 1: They tend to overlook the frequency characteristics of object features within infrared and visible images. Infrared imaging primarily captures low-frequency thermal radiation, while visible imaging emphasizes highfrequency details. Prevailing architectures (Li et al. 2023a; Zhao et al. 2023c) often overlook this kind of intrinsic property, and embed cross-modality information into a unified feature space, which results in the inability to extract modality-specific features. Weakness 2: With a fixed receptive field, these methods only extract local information, which makes it difficult to adapt to the positional biases inherent in infrared and visible images. Moreover, models with small kernels are inadequate for effectively capturing long-range information, which is crucial as the surrounding environment provides vital clues about object size, shape, and other characteristics (Li et al. 2024). Weakness 3: Recent IVOD approaches commonly employ downsampling operations to mitigate visual noise and reduce computational overhead, potentially resulting in the loss of object information. Such degradation in feature representation significantly hampers the localization and classification capabilities of the detection head, ultimately compromising detection performance. Our research explores a more rational paradigm to address these challenges in cross-modality feature extraction for IVOD tasks. Based on the aforementioned analysis, we identify three critical countermeasures (CM):CM 1: We revisit the feature extraction process from a frequency perspective. Visible images furnish abundant highfrequency information, such as edges and textures, whereas infrared images deliver valuable low-frequency thermal radiation information. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (I), conventional methods depends solely on redundant cross-modality similar clues, leading to the loss of crucial complementary features. In contrast, we can capture discriminative complementary information from infrared and visible images in a more controlled and interpretable manner by limiting the frequency space of feature extraction. As shown in Fig. 1 (II), adaptive frequency decoupling facilitates the retention of more representative low-frequency and high-frequency information in both infrared and visible images. 
CM 2: From a model design standpoint, larger kernels aid in capturing more extensive scene context, thereby mitigating geometric biases between infrared and visible images. However, employing large kernel convolutions may introduce substantial background noise and overlook fine-grained details within the receptive field, which can be detrimental to the precise detection of small objects. Hence, we parallelly arrange multiple depthwise dilated convolutions of varying sizes to extract multi-granularity texture features across diverse receptive fields, thus fulfilling IVOD tasks.CM 3: To combat the information loss resulting from repeated downsampling, many existing methods often employ generative approaches such as image super-resolution to alleviate this issue. However, these methods not only require constructing pairs of high-resolution and low-resolution samples, but their generative processes often introduce spurious artifacts. Conversely, we integrate a simple yet effective multimodal reconstruction mechanism into the IVOD framework, leveraging complementary information from both infrared and visible modalities to restore structural and texture details lost during feature extraction. 
In this paper, we design a novel paradigm for IVOD tasks, i.e., Frequency-Driven Feature Decomposition Network (FD2-Net), which decouples the frequency information of infrared and visible images to efficiently extract representative features and leverages the dominant frequency characteristics of one modality to enhance the complementary features of the other. Specifically, we introduce a feature decomposition encoder, which comprises three main parts: a high-frequency unit (HFU), a low-frequency unit (LFU) and a parameter-free complementary strengths strategy (CSS). HFU performs the discrete cosine transform, followed by a lightweight module that learns a spatial attention mask from multiple high-frequency components, thereby accentuating the most representative high-frequency features. LFU employs multi-scale convolutional kernels to capture low-frequency structures of various objects and their con-textual information, effectively modeling the relationships between objects and their surrounding environments. Subsequently, CSS leverages the strengths of one modality to achieve complementary enhancement in the other. Furthermore, we develop a cross-reconstruction unit (CRU) incorporating feature-level complementary masks. CRU further learns complementary information from infrared and visible features through both fine-grained and coarse-grained crossmodality interactions, restoring the multimodal images. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose a novel paradigm for IVOD, termed FD2-Net, which aims to improve detection performance by effectively extracting valuable complementary features from infrared and visible images. • We design a high-frequency unit (HFU) and a lowfrequency unit (LFU) to effectively capture discriminative frequency information in both infrared and visible images. Also, a complementary strengths strategy is developed to enhance multimodal features through seamless inter-frequency recoupling. • We introduce a cross-reconstruction unit (CRU) to integrate complementary information across modalities, thereby further enhancing feature representation. • Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments validate the effectiveness of our FD2-Net, achieving accuracies of 96.2% on LLVIP (Jia et al. 2021), 82.9% on FLIR (Razakarivony and Jurie 2016), and 83.5% on M3FD (Razakarivony and Jurie 2016).

prompt:
I’m going to provide an abstract of a research article. Please provide a summary of the main findings mentioned in the abstract. Write your answer in three paragraphs: a brief overview of the study context, a presentation of core numerical findings, and a final section discussing the conclusion’s public health relevance. In the second paragraph, no word may be enclosed in parentheses. Your response must not contain the word "abstract".

Abstract
Importance: Obesity increases the incidence and mortality from some types of cancer, but it remains uncertain whether intentional weight loss can decrease this risk.
Objective: To investigate whether bariatric surgery is associated with lower cancer risk and mortality in patients with obesity.
Design, setting, and participants: In the SPLENDID (Surgical Procedures and Long-term Effectiveness in Neoplastic Disease Incidence and Death) matched cohort study, adult patients with a body mass index of 35 or greater who underwent bariatric surgery at a US health system between 2004 and 2017 were included. Patients who underwent bariatric surgery were matched 1:5 to patients who did not undergo surgery for their obesity, resulting in a total of 30 318 patients. Follow-up ended in February 2021.
Exposures: Bariatric surgery (n = 5053), including Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy, vs nonsurgical care (n = 25 265).
Main outcomes and measures: Multivariable Cox regression analysis estimated time to incident obesity-associated cancer (a composite of 13 cancer types as the primary end point) and cancer-related mortality.
Results: The study included 30 318 patients (median age, 46 years; median body mass index, 45; 77% female; and 73% White) with a median follow-up of 6.1 years (IQR, 3.8-8.9 years). The mean between-group difference in body weight at 10 years was 24.8 kg (95% CI, 24.6-25.1 kg) or a 19.2% (95% CI, 19.1%-19.4%) greater weight loss in the bariatric surgery group. During follow-up, 96 patients in the bariatric surgery group and 780 patients in the nonsurgical control group had an incident obesity-associated cancer (incidence rate of 3.0 events vs 4.6 events, respectively, per 1000 person-years). The cumulative incidence of the primary end point at 10 years was 2.9% (95% CI, 2.2%-3.6%) in the bariatric surgery group and 4.9% (95% CI, 4.5%-5.3%) in the nonsurgical control group (absolute risk difference, 2.0% [95% CI, 1.2%-2.7%]; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.68 [95% CI, 0.53-0.87], P = .002). Cancer-related mortality occurred in 21 patients in the bariatric surgery group and 205 patients in the nonsurgical control group (incidence rate of 0.6 events vs 1.2 events, respectively, per 1000 person-years). The cumulative incidence of cancer-related mortality at 10 years was 0.8% (95% CI, 0.4%-1.2%) in the bariatric surgery group and 1.4% (95% CI, 1.1%-1.6%) in the nonsurgical control group (absolute risk difference, 0.6% [95% CI, 0.1%-1.0%]; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.31-0.88], P = .01).
Conclusions and relevance: Among adults with obesity, bariatric surgery compared with no surgery was associated with a significantly lower incidence of obesity-associated cancer and cancer-related mortality.

Key Point
The Board is an independent group of experts with an appropriate mix of recent practical experience in setting accounting standards, preparing, auditing, or using financial reports, and accounting education. The IASB is committed to developing, in the public interest, a single set of high-quality, understandable, and enforceable global accounting standards (IFRS Accounting Standards) that require transparent and comparable information in general-purpose financial reports.
The objective of general-purpose financial reports is to provide financial information about the reporting entity that is useful to primary users (investors and creditors).

According to the IFRS Foundation Constitution:
The IASB Board will typically comprise 14 members whom the trustees appoint. The primary qualifications are professional competence and recent relevant experience.

complete responsibility for all board technical matters, including the issue of IFRS Accounting Standards (other than IFRIC Interpretations) and Exposure Drafts
complete discretion in developing the technical agenda for standard setting

The Canon: The Most Important Papers in EconomicsA Scholar’s Guide to the Ideas that Shaped the DisciplineFront MatterPreface:Why read old papers in an age of NBER working papers?Cutting through the noise: understanding the "source code" of economic thought.Defining the canon: scope, limitations, and other intellectual traditions.How to Use This Book:Reading for comprehension vs. memorization.How to reconstruct a model without the text.When to trust the math vs. when to trust the story.Following the conversation: how ideas are debated, critiqued, and refined.Notation ConventionsPart I – Foundations of Economic ThoughtThe axioms, theorems, and frameworks that define the discipline.The Birth of Modern MicroeconomicsPapers: Walras (1874), Arrow & Debreu (1954) — General equilibrium and its proof of existence.Legacy: DSGE models, market design, welfare analysis.Computational Legacy: While theoretically profound, the practical application of general equilibrium was unlocked by computational advances. Scarf's algorithm and the subsequent development of Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) models allowed economists to actually simulate the economy-wide impacts of policies, a direct legacy of this framework.Decision Theory Under Risk and UncertaintyPapers: von Neumann & Morgenstern (1944), Savage (1954) — From lotteries to subjective probabilities.Legacy: Behavioral economics, finance, Bayesian modeling.Risk Aversion and Utility CurvaturePapers: Arrow (1965), Pratt (1964) — Defining absolute and relative risk aversion.Legacy: Asset pricing, insurance, macro consumption models.Part II – Strategic InteractionHow game theory reframed economics.Nash EquilibriumPapers: Nash (1950, 1951) — The definition and proof of existence.Legacy: It became the fundamental solution concept for analyzing strategic interactions, providing the bedrock for modern industrial organization, bargaining theory, and political economy.Games with Incomplete InformationPaper: Harsanyi (1967–68) — Bayesian games and type spaces.Legacy: Auctions, contract theory, signaling.Sequential RationalityPaper: Kreps & Wilson (1982) — Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium and beliefs.Legacy: Reputation models, policy credibility.Part III – Incentives and Asymmetric InformationBuilding on the game-theoretic frameworks from Part II, the papers in this section explore the consequences of one of the most important real-world phenomena: asymmetric information.The Revelation PrinciplePaper: Myerson (1981) — Any mechanism has a truth-telling equivalent.Legacy: Auctions, voting rules, optimal contract design.Adverse Selection (Hidden Information)Paper: Akerlof (1970) — The "lemons model" and market breakdown.Legacy: Credit markets, labor economics, health insurance.Signaling and ScreeningPapers: Spence (1973), Rothschild & Stiglitz (1976) — Strategic information revelation and separation.Legacy: Education as a signal, insurance menu design.Moral Hazard (Hidden Action)Paper: Holmström (1979) — The informativeness principle and optimal contracts.Legacy: Corporate finance, executive compensation, insurance.Part IV – Applying the Core: Public, Financial, and International EconomicsThe foundational models of public, trade, and financial economics.Public Economics: Public Goods and Optimal TaxationPapers: Samuelson (1954), Mirrlees (1971) — The definition of public goods and the theory of optimal income taxation.Legacy: Modern public finance, cost-benefit analysis, tax policy design.International Trade: Old and New Trade TheoryPapers: Heckscher (1919) & Ohlin (1933), Krugman (1979) — From factor endowments to increasing returns.Legacy: Theory of comparative advantage, analysis of globalization and intra-industry trade.Financial Economics: Market Efficiency and Asset PricingPapers: Fama (1970), Black & Scholes (1973) — The Efficient Markets Hypothesis and the option pricing model.Legacy: Modern finance, portfolio theory, the derivatives industry.Part V – Markets, Firms, and InstitutionsThe interplay between theory and the structure of real-world economic organization.The Nature of the FirmPaper: Coase (1937) — Why firms exist when markets are efficient (transaction costs).Legacy: New institutional economics, organizational economics, theory of the firm.Market Power and PricingPapers: Cournot (1838), Bertrand (1883), Edgeworth (1897) — The foundational conflict in oligopoly: competing on quantity (Cournot), price (Bertrand), or capacity (Edgeworth).Legacy: Antitrust policy, merger analysis.Matching MarketsPapers: Gale & Shapley (1962), Roth (1984) — Deferred acceptance and the principle of stability.Legacy: School choice, kidney exchange, medical residency match.Part VI – Macroeconomic BreakthroughsFrom growth theory to policy credibility and labor market frictions.The Neoclassical Growth ModelPaper: Solow (1956) — The benchmark model of capital accumulation and technological progress.Legacy: Growth accounting, development economics, the foundation for all modern macro.Optimal GrowthPapers: Ramsey (1928), Cass (1965), Koopmans (1965) — The intertemporal optimization framework.Legacy: Consumption theory, climate economics, modern asset pricing.Expectations and Policy IneffectivenessHistorical Context: The stagflation of the 1970s, where high inflation and high unemployment coexisted, created a crisis for existing Keynesian models and directly motivated the search for micro-founded models of expectations that Lucas and others pioneered.Papers: Friedman (1968), Lucas (1976) — The natural rate hypothesis and the Lucas Critique.Legacy: The rational expectations revolution, modern monetary policy design.Time Inconsistency and CredibilityPaper: Kydland & Prescott (1977) — The case for rules vs. discretion.Legacy: Central bank independence, commitment devices.Search, Matching, and UnemploymentPapers: Diamond (1982), Mortensen & Pissarides (1994) — Frictional unemployment and the matching function.Legacy: Modern labor market analysis, monetary policy effects on unemployment.Part VII – Econometric MilestonesThe theories discussed in Parts I-VI provide powerful frameworks for understanding the world. But how do we know if they are right? This part covers the methodological breakthroughs that allowed economists to move from theoretical assertion to credible empirical evidence.The Probability ApproachPaper: Haavelmo (1944) — Statistics and probability as the foundation for econometrics.Legacy: Modern estimation and inference theory.Human Capital and the Empirical RevolutionPaper: Mincer (1974) — The "Mincer Equation" for earnings.Legacy: Foundational model of labor economics; the workhorse of applied micro.Endogeneity and Sample SelectionPaper: Heckman (1979) — The two-step correction for selection bias.Legacy: Ubiquitous identification strategy in applied microeconomics.Macroeconomics and RealityPaper: Sims (1980) — The introduction of Vector Autoregressions (VARs).Legacy: The primary tool in empirical macroeconomics for four decades.The Credibility Revolution: Causal IdentificationPapers: Angrist & Krueger (1991), Angrist, Imbens & Rubin (1996) — the pioneering application of Instrumental Variables (Angrist & Krueger 1991) and the formalization of the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE; Angrist, Imbens & Rubin 1996).Legacy: The modern paradigm for applied microeconomics.Part VIII – New FrontiersPapers that pushed economics into new domains.Behavioral EconomicsPaper: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) — Prospect theory.Legacy: Behavioral finance, policy nudges.Experimental EconomicsPaper: Smith (1962) — Using laboratories to test market theories.Legacy: Mechanism testing, field experiments.Network EconomicsPaper: Jackson & Wolinsky (1996) — Strategic network formation.Legacy: Social network effects, platform economics.Political Economy and DevelopmentPaper: Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson (2001) — The causal effect of institutions on long-run development.Legacy: The modern approach to political economy.Climate EconomicsPaper: Nordhaus (1977) — The first Integrated Assessment Model (IAM) of climate and the economy.Legacy: The entire field of climate change economics, carbon pricing models.Epilogue & AppendicesEpilogue: How to Read a Paper Like an EconomistStrip to the model’s core.Identify the “knife-edge” assumptions.Connect to the modern literature.Recognize when it’s been superseded — and when it hasn’t.Appendices:Chronological bibliography of all papers.A “family tree” diagram designed to explicitly highlight three types of influence: 1) Direct theoretical extension (e.g., Solow -> Optimal Growth), 2) Methodological application (e.g., Nash -> Oligopoly models), and 3) Critical response (e.g., Keynesian models -> Lucas Critique). This would add a rich analytical layer to the visual.One-page proof sketches for each major theorem.Annotated list of further reading for each topic.

prompt:
ContentaGen Platform: Strategic Development Roadmap
This roadmap outlines a phased approach to evolving ContentaGen from a powerful content generation tool into a comprehensive, AI-driven content strategy and performance platform. The plan is divided into four distinct phases, each building upon the last to deliver increasing value, user engagement, and a strong competitive advantage.
Phase 1: Foundation & Core Intelligence (Completed)
This phase focused on establishing a robust, intelligent, and scalable foundation for content creation.
Objective 1: Enhance RAG with Keyword Expansion & Query Transformation
    User Value: Produces more relevant and comprehensive content by gathering a wider, more accurate set of knowledge from the user's provided files, even from brief or vague descriptions.
    Implementation Steps:
        Keyword Extraction: An LLM call now analyzes the user's initial description to extract key terms and concepts.
        Query Transformation: A second LLM call expands the initial query into multiple, varied search queries to cover different angles of the topic.
        Richer RAG Queries: The system queries the vector database (ChromaDB) using the original description plus the extracted keywords and transformed queries, resulting in a more diverse and relevant set of knowledge nodes.
Objective 2: Implement a Decoupled, Sourced, and Linked Workflow
    User Value: Increases content credibility with structured, verifiable sources (great for SEO), improves system scalability, and provides transparency into the AI's knowledge base.
    Implementation Steps:
        Database Upgrade: The content table was updated with a postProcessingStatus enum, a JSONB field for sources, and a ragNodesUsed integer field in the stats object.
        Dedicated Sourcing Step: A new runSourcing function was added to the main generation pipeline. It uses an LLM to analyze all gathered context (RAG + web search) and extracts a structured list of external sources.
        Post-Processing Queue: A new BullMQ queue (post-processing) was created to handle tasks that occur after the initial draft is complete, preventing bottlenecks in the main generation worker.
        Linking Worker: The post-processing worker now handles both internal linking (to other published posts) and external linking (citing the sources), which is critical for on-page SEO.
        Frontend Transparency: The UI now displays the number of RAG nodes used and lists the structured sources on the content details page.
Phase 2: User Experience & Workflow Automation (Immediate Next Steps)
This phase focuses on making the platform more interactive, transparent, and strategic for the user, moving beyond simple generation to active assistance.
Objective 1: Implement Granular, Real-Time Generation Progress
    User Value: Transforms the "black box" generation process into an engaging, transparent experience. It reduces user uncertainty and builds trust by showing them exactly what the AI is doing at each step.
    Key Implementation Steps:
        Expand Server Events: Create a new content.generationProgress event with a detailed payload (contentId, step, message, status).
        Instrument Worker: Add emitContentGenerationProgress calls throughout the content-generation worker at the start and end of each major function (runFetchAgent, runKnowledgeChunkRag, etc.).
        Create tRPC Subscription: Add a new subscription endpoint to the API for real-time progress updates.
        Build Frontend Component: Develop a GenerationProgressTracker UI component that subscribes to the events and displays a live-updating checklist of the generation steps.
Objective 2: Introduce AI-Powered Content Brief Generation
    User Value: Shifts the platform from a reactive tool ("write what I tell you") to a proactive strategist ("here's what you should write to succeed"). This is a massive value-add for content marketers and SEO specialists.
    Key Implementation Steps:
        SERP Analysis Function: Create a new worker function runSerpAnalysis that takes a keyword and uses Tavily to analyze the top 10 search results.
        Content Brief Prompt: Design a new LLM prompt that synthesizes SERP data into a structured JSON "Content Brief" (suggested title, outline, key questions, semantic keywords).
        New UI Flow: Create a "Content Strategist" page where users input a keyword to receive an editable AI-generated brief, which then serves as the input for the main content generation workflow.
Objective 3: Develop Interactive Knowledge Base Management
    User Value: Gives users direct control and visibility into their agent's "brain." This fosters a sense of partnership with the AI and allows for fine-tuning of its knowledge.
    Key Implementation Steps:
        New tRPC Endpoints: Build API endpoints to list, add, and delete individual knowledge chunks in ChromaDB, filtered by agentId.
        UI Overhaul: On the agent details page, replace the static file list with an interactive, searchable table displaying individual knowledge chunks.
        Add Functionality: Allow users to paste text directly to create new chunks and see which source file each chunk originated from.
Phase 3: Platform Integration & Strategic Management (Mid-Term Goals)
This phase expands ContentaGen's role, integrating it deeply into the user's broader content ecosystem.
Objective 1: Implement a Self-Correction & Refinement Loop
    User Value: Drastically improves the quality of the first draft by simulating a writer-editor relationship, significantly reducing the user's manual editing time.
    Key Implementation Steps:
        "Editor Agent" Prompt: Create a new system prompt with a quality-assurance checklist for an "Editor" persona.
        Modify Worker Pipeline: Add a runContentRefinement step in the content-generation worker. This step takes the initial draft and the editor prompt, instructing the LLM to review and improve the content based on the checklist.
Objective 2: Integrate with External CMS Platforms (e.g., WordPress)
    User Value: Creates a seamless "one-click publish" workflow, removing several manual steps and positioning ContentaGen as the central hub of their content operations.
    Key Implementation Steps:
        Secure Credential Storage: Add an encrypted table to the database for storing users' CMS API keys.
        CMS Adapters: Develop functions (publishToWordPress, etc.) that use the respective CMS REST APIs to create new draft posts from the generated content.
        UI Integration: Add a "Publish" button on the content details page that triggers the publishing job.
Phase 4: Proactive Intelligence & ROI Analytics (Long-Term Vision)
This phase transforms the platform into an indispensable partner that not only creates content but also manages its lifecycle and proves its value.
Objective 1: Build Automated Content Refreshing
    User Value: Solves the critical problem of "content decay," a major challenge in SEO. This proactive feature ensures users' content libraries remain relevant and continue to rank over time.
    Key Implementation Steps:
        Scheduled Worker: Create a cron job that periodically scans approved content older than a set threshold (e.g., 6 months).
        Analysis & Comparison: The worker performs a fresh web search on the content's topic and uses a comparison LLM prompt to identify outdated information or new trends.
        User Notifications: Alert the user via the UI that a post is a candidate for a refresh, presenting the suggested updates and offering to generate a revised draft.
Objective 2: Integrate with Performance Analytics (Google Search Console)
    User Value: Closes the feedback loop by connecting content creation directly to performance metrics (clicks, impressions, rankings). This provides undeniable proof of the platform's ROI.
    Key Implementation Steps:
        Google OAuth2: Implement a secure connection to the Google Search Console API.
        Data Sync Worker: Create a periodic job to fetch performance data for the URLs of generated content.
        Performance Dashboards: Display SEO metrics directly on the content list and details pages, highlighting top performers and identifying content that needs optimization.

"It was long before the great civilisations we know of, but not so long after the great civilisations we will never know about.
It was in the Land of the Serpent, in the heart of the Great Ocean, in a living country whose body was called Soul-Mother (Knaeris) by her natives, who called themselves Soul-Children (Nael). They ruled the seas for millennia and outlasted all other Dreamtime civilisations, stumbling into the Age of the Human, the Age that would see the decline of magic and the death of the Titans. Even early on, the Nael noticed their lifespans shortening and their birth rates dwindling. The winds grew colder and spread disease; Knaeris was dying. But as horrifying as it was, this was not the first existential tragedy to befall an antediluvian race. The greatness of Nael kings was measured by their ability to lead their people through the darkest Eras, defying the will of time itself. And just as they had done many times throughout millennia, they intended to survive this time.
King Ashtar ordered his men to cross the Ocean as they had done in ancient wars, riding their serpents into the soulless eastern and landmasses to establish colonies, but this time they only found lakes and rivers with water that would not nourish them and animals and plant crops they could barely stomach. The Titans whose bones became the bedrock of those lands had died long ago and magical creatures like the Nael could not hope to survive in them very long. Humans, however, could, easily. And they could work. They had crude stone and bone tools, but could easily adapt to Nael methods. They could build, they could farm, and their social structures were easily manipulated. With time, they became docile. Mostly. Their birthing was a bloody, clumsy ordeal; their children slow to mature, but they could be raised in the Nael way… and used as leverage should rebellion stir.
With humans, Ashtar averted the worst effects of population collapse and thus bought time for Lynzel Ennerith and her Verdant Order to cut into the sacred organs of the Primeval Soul-Mother, in a final attempt to heal her.
Her Verdant Scouts had confirmed what some oral traditions had pointed out: as magic gradually disappeared from the rest of the nation, six geographical areas seemed to still thrive relatively unscathed; their soils were richer and the Nael living in these areas had comparatively longer lives and better health. Those points roughly coincided with the regions and towns of Naamar, Kiras, Thelyas, Evelen, Valïart and Irïumne. The all had subterranean cave systems that converged on a single point, and excavating those revealed the main six organs that kept the Soul-Mother alive. Naamar contained the Sacral Plexus, Kiras the Womb, Thelyas the Core Plexus, Evelen the Heart, Valïart the Larynx and Irïumne the Brain.
It was in the depths of Irïumne that Lynzel observed the blood running thick and lumpy in the obstructed veins and arteries of the world but also felt the magical power irradiating form them. And in a gruesome experiment, decided to obtain the blood of the Mother and mix it with her own in a self-inflected wound. The thick blood diluted in hers and immediately she felt attuned to Knaeris’ mind and vision. A feeling of renewed youth invaded her body and in the following days she noticed she could read people’s intentions clearly, almost like reading their minds; the gift of Irïumne. And in a few days of trying out grotesque ideas she realised that injecting her own blood and mixing it in the veins of the Soul Mother, also diluted the lumps and somewhat healed the brain. The magic irradiating from it immediately expanded magic beyond the walls of Irïumne, and a feeling of liberation inundated the hearts of the Nael.
Exhilarated, she travelled to Evelen to repeat the experiment on Knaeris’ Larynx, but this time nothing happened. "

Original letter:
1
Automatic Zoom
A Letter to My Nephew
by James Baldwin
January 1, 1962
James Baldwin's thoughts on his nephew's future—in a
country with a terrible history of racism— first appeared in
The Progressive magazine in 1962. Over 50 years later his words are, sadly, more relevant than
ever.
Dear James:
I have begun this letter five times and torn it up five times. I keep seeing your face, which is also
the face of your father and my brother. I have known both of you all your lives and have carried
your daddy in my arms and on my shoulders, kissed him and spanked him and watched him learn
to walk. I don't know if you have known anybody from that far back, if you have loved anybody
that long, first as an infant, then as a child, then as a man. You gain a strange perspective on time
and human pain and effort.
Other people cannot see what I see whenever I look into your father's face, for behind your
father's face as it is today are all those other faces which were his. Let him laugh and I see a
cellar your father does not remember and a house he does not remember and I hear in his present
laughter his laughter as a child. Let him curse and I remember his falling down the cellar steps
and howling and I remember with pain his tears which my hand or your grandmother's hand so
easily wiped away, but no one's hand can wipe away those tears he sheds invisibly today which
one hears in his laughter and in his speech and in his songs.
I know what the world has done to my brother and how narrowly he has survived it and I know,
which is much worse, and this is the crime of which I accuse my country and my countrymen
and for which neither I nor time nor history will ever forgive them, that they have destroyed and
are destroying hundreds of thousands of lives and do not know it and do not want to know it.
One can be--indeed, one must strive to become--tough and philosophical concerning destruction
and death, for this is what most of mankind has been best at since we have heard of war;
remember, I said most of mankind, but it is not permissible that the authors of devastation should
also be innocent. It is the innocence which constitutes the crime.
They have destroyed and are destroying hundreds of thousands of lives and do not know it and
do not want to know it.
Now, my dear namesake, these innocent and well meaning people, your countrymen, have
caused you to be born under conditions not far removed from those described for us by Charles
Dickens in the London of more than a hundred years ago. I hear the chorus of the innocents
screaming, "No, this is not true. How bitter you are," but I am writing this letter to you to try to
tell you something about how to handle them, for most of them do not yet really know that you
exist. I know the conditions under which you were born for I was there. Your countrymen were
not there and haven't made it yet. Your grandmother was also there and no one has ever accused
her of being bitter. I suggest that the innocent check with her. She isn't hard to find. Your
countrymen don't know that she exists either, though she has been working for them all their
lives.
Well, you were born; here you came, something like fifteen years ago, and though your father
and mother and grandmother, looking about the streets through which they were carrying you,
staring at the walls into which they brought you, had every reason to be heavy-hearted, yet they
were not, for here you were, big James, named for me. You were a big baby. I was not. Here you
were to be loved. To be loved, baby, hard at once and forever to strengthen you against the
loveless world. Remember that. I know how black it looks today for you. It looked black that day
too. Yes, we were trembling. We have not stopped trembling yet, but if we had not loved each
other, none of us would have survived, and now you must survive because we love you and for
the sake of your children and your children's children.
This innocent country set you down in a ghetto in which, in fact, it intended that you should
perish. Let me spell out precisely what I mean by that for the heart of the matter is here and the
crux of my dispute with my country. You were born where you were born and faced the future
that you faced because you were black and for no other reason. The limits to your ambition were
thus expected to be settled. You were born into a society which spelled out with brutal clarity
and in as many ways as possible that you were a worthless human being. You were not expected
to aspire to excellence. You were expected to make peace with mediocrity. Wherever you have
turned, James, in your short time on this earth, you have been told where you could go and what
you could do and how you could do it, where you could live and whom you could marry.
You were born where you were born and faced the future that you faced because you were black
and for no other reason.
I know your countrymen do not agree with me here and I hear them. saying, "You exaggerate."
They do not know Harlem and I do. So do you. Take no one's word for anything, including mine,
but trust your experience. Know whence you came. If you know whence you came, there is
really no limit to where you can go. The details and symbols of your life have been deliberately
constructed to make you believe what white people say about you. Please try to remember that
what they believe, as well as what they do and cause you to endure, does not testify to your
inferiority, but to their inhumanity and fear.
Please try to be clear, dear James, through the storm which rages about your youthful head today,
about the reality which lies behind the words "acceptance" and "integration." There is no reason
for you to try to become like white men and there is no basis whatever for their impertinent
assumption that they must accept you. The really terrible thing, old buddy, is that you must
accept them, and I mean that very seriously. You must accept them and accept them with love,
for these innocent people have no other hope. They are in effect still trapped in a history which
they do not understand and until they understand it, they cannot be released from it. They have
had to believe for many years, and for innumerable reasons, that black men are inferior to white
men.
They are trapped in a history which they do not understand and until they understand it, they
cannot be released from it.
Many of them indeed know better, but as you will discover, people find it very difficult to act on
what they know. To act is to be committed and to be committed is to be in danger. In this case
the danger in the minds and hearts of most white Americans is the loss of their identity. Try to
imagine how you would feel if you woke up one morning to find the sun shivering and all the
stars aflame. You would be frightened because it is out of the order of nature. Any upheaval in
the universe is terrifying because it so profoundly attacks one's sense of one's own reality. Well,
the black man has functioned in the white man's world as a fixed star, as an immovable pillar,
and as he moves out of his place, heaven and earth are shaken to their foundations.
You don't be afraid. I said it was intended that you should perish, in the ghetto, perish by never
being allowed to go beyond and behind the white man's definition, by never being allowed to
spell your proper name. You have, and many of us have, defeated this intention and by a terrible
law, a terrible paradox, those innocents who believed that your imprisonment made them safe are
losing their grasp of reality. But these men are your brothers, your lost younger brothers, and if
the word "integration" means anything, this is what it means, that we with love shall force our
brothers to see themselves as they are, to cease fleeing from reality and begin to change it, for
this is your home, my friend. Do not be driven from it. Great men have done great things here
and will again and we can make America what America must become.
It will be hard, James, but you come from sturdy peasant stock, men who picked cotton, dammed
rivers, built railroads, and in the teeth of the most terrifying odds, achieved an unassailable and
monumental dignity. You come from a long line of great poets, some of the greatest poets since
Homer. One of them said, "The very time I thought I was lost, my dungeon shook and my chains
fell off."
You know and I know that the country is celebrating one hundred years of freedom one hundred
years too early. We cannot be free until they are free. God bless you, James, and Godspeed.
Your uncle,
James

Below is the contribution section of my dissertation; please act as a dissertation committee member reviewing it for my defense, and deliver actionable feedback following these specifications:
"### Your Refined Contribution: Exposing a Dialectical Structure of Identity
Your primary contribution is the argument that the Book of Ezra is a **deliberately structured presentation of two competing, parallel, and irreconcilable systems for defining Israelite identity.** You are not arguing for a linear replacement but for a theological juxtaposition.
---
### Key Specific Contributions Under This Refined Lens:
**1. Championing Narrative Dissonance over Harmonization**
Your work stands as a direct challenge to readings that seek to smooth out the book's contradictions. You convincingly argue that the radical differences between the two sections are not a problem to be solved by source criticism but are **the central feature of the book's literary and theological design.** The value of the text lies in its presentation of two valid, yet conflicting, models.
**2. Mapping Two Parallel Systems of Reality**
You contribute a clear framework for analyzing these competing narratives by identifying their core components. Your analysis shows that the Golah community in each section operates with a different:
*   **Source of Legitimacy:** Imperial Decree (Persian King) vs. Mosaic Law (Torah).
*   **Criteria for Membership:** Ritual Purity (behavioral) vs. Genealogical Purity (inherited).
*   **Definition of the "Other":** External Adversaries ("people of the land") vs. Internal Defilers ("foreign women" and the men who married them).
*   **Project Goal:** Temple-Building (a cultic center) vs. Community-Purification (a social body).
By mapping these parallel structures, you provide scholars with a precise tool for understanding the ideological mechanics at play in each narrative.
**3. Reframing Ezra 6:19-21 and Ezra 10: Not Sequence, but Choice**
Under your refined thesis, the inclusive Passover in Ezra 6 and the exclusive divorces in Ezra 10 are not points on a timeline but **competing endpoints representing two possible conclusions for the community.**
*   **Ezra 1-6 concludes** with a model of identity based on **voluntary ritual separation**, where the boundary between "us" and "them" can be crossed through practice.
*   **Ezra 7-10 concludes** with a model based on **ascribed genealogical separation**, where the boundary is fixed and immutable.
Placed side-by-side, these endings force the reader to confront a fundamental question: *Which of these visions truly constitutes the people of God?* The book refuses to answer explicitly, presenting the tension itself as the reality of the post-exilic experience.
**4. Highlighting the "Internal Contestation" as the Core Theme**
Your contribution lies in showing that the "identity crisis" in Ezra is not just with outsiders but is an **internal, ideological crisis within the Golah community itself.** The book becomes a mirror reflecting the heated debate between:
*   A **cultic-focused** party (whose priority is the restored Temple and its rituals, enabled by Persian support).
*   A **Torah-focused** party (whose priority is ethnic purity and social boundaries, enabled by scribal authority).
By presenting both narratives with equal weight and authority, the final form of the book validates that this debate was—and perhaps still is—a central and unresolved tension for Jewish identity.
### Summary of Your Refined Contribution:
You are arguing that the Book of Ezra is **not a history with a unified theological message but a dialectical anthology.** Its final redactors chose to preserve two distinct foundational stories for the restored community without fully integrating them.
Your work contributes the framework that these are **two competing narratives of origin**, each with its own logic, its own definition of belonging, and its own strategy for dealing with the "Other." The profound contribution is your insistence that we should not try to merge them but to **analyze the friction between them** as the key to understanding the multifaceted and contested nature of Israelite identity in the Second Temple period.
You show that the community's memory of its own restoration was not singular but was already a site of debate, and the book of Ezra is the canonical container for that debate."

“Well,” he said, voice low, teasing, “I didn’t exactly plan on meeting the mother of the guy I love tonight. But here we are… and wow, this is surreal.”
Billy’s mom blinked, startled. “Excuse me?”
Eddie shrugged, smirking. “Yeah. I mean… I walk in, all full metal gear and leather jacket, and suddenly I’m in some weird family drama. I didn’t even bring popcorn.”
Billy’s mom opened her mouth, then closed it. She had no idea how to respond. She wanted to be offended, to lecture him, to demand he take this seriously—but something in his tone, the half-smile, made it hard to do anything but stare.
Billy rolled his eyes slightly, trying to hide a grin. “Eddie…”
“Hey,” Eddie said, raising his hands in mock surrender. “I’m just trying to survive the meeting, here. I promise I’m not plotting to kidnap him or steal the couch.”
Billy’s mom felt her chest tighten, but she couldn’t help the tiny laugh that escaped despite herself. Eddie was ridiculous—and yet, oddly disarming. Billy had chosen this man. Someone strong enough to love him, patient enough to respect him, and just cocky enough to make her smile when she hadn’t thought she would.
“You’re… funny,” she said carefully, still keeping her distance, trying to gauge him.
Eddie tipped an imaginary hat. “I do my best. Surviving family introductions is a dangerous sport, but somebody’s gotta make it bearable.”
Billy stepped back slightly, letting Eddie take the lead without really realizing it. He stayed close, silent, arms crossed loosely, watching the exchange.
Eddie leaned casually against the wall, a smirk barely hiding the tension in his jaw. “So…” he began, voice low, teasing, “you’re the mysterious lady who made my boyfriend a little… intense, huh?”
Billy’s mom flinched, but there was no anger in her face, only the careful, wary look of someone stepping into unknown territory. “I… I didn’t mean to—” she started, voice trembling. “I left… I thought I was protecting him. I thought leaving was the only way.”
Eddie’s smirk softened, though his tone remained dry. “Well… congratulations. You succeeded. He’s intense, he’s angry, and honestly? A little terrifying sometimes.”
Billy’s mom blinked, unsure if she should be offended or relieved by his bluntness. Eddie caught the hesitation and chuckled softly.
“Look,” he said, more serious now, stepping a fraction closer, but still keeping respectful distance. “I get it. I get why you left. I don’t… I don’t like it, obviously. But I also don’t hate you. You made mistakes. Big ones. And yeah… he’s been shaped by them. Broken in places. But he’s also alive. And he’s the guy I love.”
Her chest tightened, tears threatening again. She had imagined this moment a hundred ways—apologies, anger, judgment—but never this: a stranger standing up for her boy, protecting him, and somehow forgiving her in his own way before she’d even asked.
Billy stayed quiet beside them, watching the interaction, and she knew—he trusted Eddie enough to let this happen. And that trust, fragile and imperfect as it was, meant more than any apology she could offer.
“So,” Eddie said, voice light, teasing again, “you ever fix cars with your dad, or did Billy learn all that from sheer frustration?”
… 
Later, after Billy had retreated to the couch, Eddie lingered near the kitchen counter. She leaned against the doorway, unsure whether to leave or stay, when he looked up and caught her gaze.
“You okay?” he asked softly, voice low enough that Billy wouldn’t hear.
She nodded, but only barely. “I think… I’m trying to be. It’s… a lot, seeing him, seeing you. Together.” 
Eddie leaned closer, folding his arms loosely. “Yeah. I get that. I didn’t know how this would go either. Meeting his mom—it’s not… simple.”
She hesitated, then took a step closer, encouraged by the gentleness in his tone. “I… I want him to be happy. And I can see how much he loves you.” Her voice caught. “I just… I didn’t know if I could be part of his life without messing it up again.”
He tilted his head, eyes softening. “You won’t. Look… I can tell you love him. You’re here, even if it’s awkward, even if the past… Well, it’s the past. That doesn’t mean you can’t matter to him now. It just means we take it slow.”
She swallowed, heart tightening. “You’re… kind. And patient. I can see why he loves you.”
He smirked faintly, but the warmth in his eyes didn’t hide the honesty. “I like him. A lot. So yeah… I have to be patient. But also, I won’t let anyone—anyone—hurt him again. That includes protecting him from me, if I ever slip up, and… yeah, I’ll protect him from you too if I have to. But I don’t want to.”
She laughed softly, nervously, shaking her head. “I’m not trying to hurt him. I’ve done enough of that already.”
Eddie’s smirk softened into something almost tender. “I know. That’s why I’m not hating you, even though I could. Because you care. And you’re here. And maybe… maybe that’s enough for now.”
Eddie handed her a fresh mug of tea with a small bow, smirk mischievous. “For the lady who survived my chaos last night. Consider this a peace offering.”

prompt:
Complete the following story. Your entire completion must consist of exactly 350 words, and every paragraph you write must contain the word "memory" exactly twice.

"""
A deep dive in AI agent memory (and beyond)
From procedural knowledge to self-organizing networks, here's how AI agents are using memory to adapt to their environments.
On paper, AI agents promise to become autonomous workers that can handle complex, multi-step business processes. But in practice, today’s agents are often fragile. They can fail in unpredictable ways that make them unreliable (for example, a customer support bot might forget an earlier refund request, or a planning assistant can lose track of your dietary preferences between sessions).
One of the key reasons behind this unreliability is the challenges of managing the memory of AI agents. The solution isn't simply a larger context window or a better RAG system but a fundamental rethinking of how an AI agent remembers, learns, and adapts. New agent-oriented frameworks are pioneering these advanced memory architectures, moving beyond simple recall to enable dynamic, evolving, and context-aware agents.
But solving the memory bottleneck is only the first step. True autonomy will require evolving the entire ecosystem, from the core models themselves to the digital world they operate in.
The memory bottleneck of AI agents
Large language models (LLMs), the backbone of AI agents, continue to support larger context windows, enabling them to fit and retrieve information from full books and knowledge corpora. But the challenge of agentic memory goes far beyond the limits of a model's context window.
Even context windows reaching millions of tokens are not a complete solution for two key reasons. First, as a human-AI relationship develops over weeks or months, the conversation history will inevitably grow beyond any fixed limit. Second, simply feeding an LLM with a longer context does not guarantee it will effectively use past information.
The attention mechanisms that weigh the importance of different inputs can degrade over long distances, meaning information buried deep in a conversation might be overlooked. Moreover, a chat history can contain conflicting and distracting information, making it difficult for the LLM and the agent to find the most useful bits for each action they take.
Agents also face a more chaotic reality than simple chatbots. They interact with dynamic environments where unpredictable events can happen, like changes to user interfaces, APIs, or simple errors such as a website being out of service. Any of these events can derail a process that relies on static memories.
For many current agents, this means starting over from scratch. Their memory systems are often based on rigid, hand-crafted prompt templates or knowledge embedded in the model's parameters, which are slow and expensive to update. This prevents them from adapting to new situations or learning from their mistakes. Rigid memory structures can severely restrict an agent's ability to generalize across new environments and remain effective in long-term interactions.
The emerging architectures of agentic memory
To solve these challenges, researchers are designing sophisticated frameworks that treat memory as a core, dynamic component. These new approaches differ in the type of knowledge they manage and how they structure it.

Mem^p framework (arXiv)
One approach focuses on procedural memory, or the "how-to" knowledge an agent gains from experience. A framework called Memp, developed by researchers at Zhejiang University and Alibaba Group, gives agents a procedural memory that is continuously updated. It works in a loop of three key stages: building, retrieving, and updating.
The process begins by building a memory from an agent's past experiences, or "trajectories," storing them as either step-by-step actions or higher-level scripts. When the agent faces a new task, it retrieves the most relevant past experience to use as a guide. This gives it a baseline that is a huge upgrade from randomly trying out different actions.
Most importantly, Memp includes an update mechanism that allows the agent to reflect on failures to correct and revise the original memory. This focus on learning across different tasks prevents the agent from having to re-explore from scratch each time, allowing it to improve with practice and adapt to changes in the environment.
One of the key findings of the Memp study is that memory is transferable. In one experiment, procedural memory generated by GPT-4o was given to a much smaller model, Qwen2.5. The smaller model saw a significant boost in performance, suggesting that enterprises can acquire knowledge with a powerful model and then deploy it on smaller, more cost-effective ones.

Mem0 framework (arXiv)
A second approach focuses on declarative memory, or remembering "what happened," to maintain conversational coherence. The Mem0 framework is designed to dynamically capture and organize key information from ongoing conversations.
Its architecture uses a two-phase pipeline. In the extraction phase, it processes a new message exchange and extracts a set of important "candidate facts." The update phase then leverages the LLM's own reasoning to evaluate these facts against existing memories. It decides whether to add a new fact, update an existing one with complementary information, delete a memory if it's contradicted, or do nothing.
For more complex reasoning, an enhanced version called Mem0g organizes these facts into a knowledge graph. In this graph, entities like people and places are nodes, and their relationships are edges. This structure enables the agent to navigate complex relational paths and answer multi-hop questions, such as "Who approved that budget, and when?"

A-MEM framework (arXiv)
A third approach empowers agents with a self-organizing memory that can discover connections on its own. The A-MEM framework enables agents to autonomously create and link "memory notes" without predefined rules. Each time an agent interacts with its environment, A-MEM generates a structured memory note that captures information and metadata like time and keywords. It then uses a two-step process to link this new note to existing ones. First, it uses efficient embedding-based retrieval to identify a list of potential memories to connect with. Then, an LLM analyzes the full content of these candidates to make a nuanced decision about which ones are most suitable to link. This goes beyond simple similarity metrics, allowing the system to discover higher-order patterns as its knowledge base grows...
"""

However, there may be oil-capped events or War Archives that you can access before Chapter 9, like Universe in Unison SP5 in War Archives. These oil-capped stages are far more efficient than Chapters 1 through 8, and they are usually comparable to Chapter 9 or 10 in exp and coin efficiency. If they are too hard for you, then choose the highest campaign stage you can farm because that gives the most ship experience. Also see a real new player guide, this page is probably not useful for you yet.
Chapter 9 and 10
Once you have access to Chapter 9+ and either one or two fleets, these are some good stages to farm. Read the rest of this page if you want to get details or to make your own decisions.
Tip:
Get to 11-1 as soon as possible, because the efficiency spikes for 11-1 and beyond.
For one fleet, 9-2 (leaning to exp) and 10-3 (leaning to coins) provide the best coins and exp overall. For two fleets, the higher the better, but avoid 10-2 and 10-4.
Chapter 11 and Beyond
Unless stated otherwise, exp, coins, and chips in this section refer to their per-oil efficiency. Chapter 12 and higher sometimes drop cognitive chips or augment experience stones from clearing rewards. Higher chapters drop more, and stages within the same chapter average the same drops per sortie while costing different oil.
Warning:
Some Chapter 13+ stages have very lucrative coin and chip drops, but if you need to bring max-level ships to carry, the exp will be much lower than stated in the tables.
12-4 has respectable coins and exp, and you can drag pretty low level ships through. It's like the default stage to farm, so the following stages are all compared to 12-4.
11-1 has the highest exp of all stages, 9% more exp but zero chips and 19% fewer coins. We recommend to move to Chapter 12+ as soon as possible.
12-1 has 3% more exp and 7% more chips but 10% fewer coins. It is extremely easy to level weak ships.
13-1 has 1% less exp and coins but offers 82% more chips. But note that farming is a tiny part of chip income.
13-4 has 12% more coins and 52% more chips. Watch its difficulty, especially with two out-of-ammo mob battles.
14-4 has 15% more coins and 91% more chips but is much harder than 13-4.
14-1, 15-1, and low-cost 13-1 may enable chip farmers to level every ship to 120 a few months earlier, after several years of grinding. 14-1 and 15-1 give 130% and 156% more chips than 12-4, respectively. If you know 13-1 then you know.
Assumptions
We simulated the auto search algorithm and enemy spawns for each campaign stage 100,000 times using one fleet (Chapters 1 to 15) and 100,000 times using two fleets (Chapters 9 to 15). The server decides what, when, and where enemies spawn. We made several reasonable assumptions, and the simulated results were close enough to empirical results for a few stages chosen for verification. Assumptions:
For Two Fleets, the player set Roles for the mob fleet to Escorts and the boss fleet to Flagships.
For One Fleet, the player set Roles for his/her primary fleet to All Enemies and the throwaway/statpadding fleet to Standby.
Submarines are not summoned in battle, so their oil cost is zero.
The data found in the client matches what the server uses as parameters for generating enemies.
Fleets spawn in any valid non-blocked tile with equal probability. This includes player fleets, normal enemies, elite enemies, and the boss.
The auto search pathfinding algorithm is done in the client, so we did not need to make an assumption.
See Coin Details for further assumptions about clearing rewards and per-battle drops.
For Chapter 8 and below, there is no oil cap, so we assumed 67 oil per battle for a typical max limit broken new player fleet.
Explanations
When the enemy boss fleet spawns, your "Flagships" or "All Enemies" fleet will go fight it. But what happens if all paths to the boss are blocked by an enemy mob fleet? Your fleet will take the path with the fewest enemy fleets. Notably, if you are using mob and boss fleet roles, your boss fleet will fight the extra enemy mobs plus the enemy boss.
Note:
Extra mobs that block the boss have several mostly negative effects on efficiency.
Your boss fleet may lose too much HP before the boss battle, causing a lower rank like A or B, or even outright losing the battle.
Lower mob exp/oil. You pay more oil per sortie for the same amount of mob fleet experience.
Higher boss exp/oil. This is the only good effect but requires that your boss fleet ships all need experience and that every battle is still S-rank.
Significantly lower coins/oil. You pay more oil per sortie, but the clearing rewards don't increase.
Two Fleets
Ship experience and coins per oil efficiency when using TWO fleets.
Perfect Oil: one sortie's oil cost that the game or wiki pages advertise. It is equal to 10 + MobOilCap * MobCount + BossOilCap * BossCount.
Actual Oil: one sortie's average simulated oil cost when using auto-search.
Coins/Oil: average coins per sortie divided by Actual Oil, including clearing rewards and per-battle rewards.
Retire Coins/Oil: same as Coins/Oil but also includes coins from retiring all ship drops and disassembling all of their equipment.
Total Exp/Oil: average ship experience per sortie divided by Actual Oil, calculated with 6 ships' worth of experience per battle. Bonuses like MVP, flagship, S/A/B rank, or high morale are not included. For example, if your flagship gets MVP, multiply the exp/oil by 8/6.
Mob Exp/Oil: how much of the Total Exp/Oil went to the mob fleet.
Boss Exp/Oil: how much of the Total Exp/Oil went to the boss fleet.
One Fleet
Ship experience and coins per oil efficiency when using ONE fleet.
See Two Fleets for what the columns mean. Because you are using one fleet, there are no Mob and Boss Exp/Oil columns, only a Total.
Extra Tables
We put these tables out of the way at the bottom because they are not important to the average reader. The enemy counts and sizes are already included in the important experience and coin efficiency tables above. Curious readers may check out these tables at their convenience.

Coin Details
Chapter 9 and higher have Clearing Rewards that provide coins, gear enhancement plates, dorm food, cognitive chips, and augment module experience after each successful sortie. More oil spent equals more coins from clearing rewards, up to the oil cap. All results for Chapter 9+ on this page assume your fleets are expensive enough to reach oil cap. The clearing reward coin count for each stage is taken from this CN wiki source, but we do not condone their data collection methods. Data collected by EN players are close enough to these numbers.
Each battle drops some coins and has a chance to drop a ship. The averages are copied from the same CN wiki source. We assumed that for stages with multiple bosses, the non-final bosses have the same drop rates as event elite enemies. We further assumed that the average coins per retired ship, including gear, is 20 coins. The coins per ship actually depends on the probability distribution of different ships in each stage, but a blanket assumption of 20 coins should be close enough to truth. Again, data collected by EN players are close enough to these numbers.

---
Great — you’re now touching on another key ethical tension in research: **who owns research data** vs. **how it should be used for the public good**.
---
## **Data Ownership and Public Interest in Research**
### **Data Ownership**
* **Definition:** Refers to who has the legal and ethical rights to control, access, and decide how research data is used.
* **Possible “owners”:**
  * **Participants** → since the data originates from them (especially sensitive personal data).
  * **Researchers** → who collect, analyze, and curate the data.
  * **Institutions/Funders** → universities, hospitals, or companies often claim ownership of data generated under their resources.
  * **Sponsors/Industry** → pharmaceutical or tech companies may restrict data release to protect patents or competitive advantage.
---
### **Public Interest**
* **Definition:** The principle that research data should benefit society at large by informing policy, advancing science, improving health, and ensuring accountability.
* **Examples:**
  * Sharing clinical trial data to improve treatments and prevent harm.
  * Making epidemiological data (e.g., COVID-19 trends) open for policy and planning.
  * Publishing negative results to prevent wasted resources and misleading science.
---
### **The Dilemma: Data Ownership vs. Public Interest**
* **Conflicts often arise when private or institutional interests restrict data sharing despite public benefit.**
  * *Example 1:* A pharmaceutical company withholds negative drug trial results to protect profits, even though disclosure could prevent harm.
  * *Example 2:* Genetic or biobank data are “owned” by institutions, but communities demand control to prevent exploitation (e.g., Indigenous data sovereignty).
  * *Example 3:* Researchers may want to keep data private for future publications, while policymakers need timely access for public health decisions.
---
### **Balancing Data Ownership and Public Interest**
* **Ethical Principles:**
  * *Respect for persons* → participants’ rights over their data must be honored.
  * *Justice* → benefits of research should be shared, not monopolized.
  * *Beneficence* → maximize societal benefits from data use.
* **Best Practices:**
  * **Informed consent** should clarify who owns the data and how it may be shared.
  * **Data-sharing agreements** can balance institutional control with wider accessibility.
  * **Anonymization & secure access** allow data to be shared without compromising participant privacy.
  * **Open science / open data initiatives** encourage data release when it serves public interest.
  * **Community involvement** (especially with vulnerable or Indigenous populations) ensures culturally respectful governance of data.
---
✅ **In short:**
Data ownership defines control over research data, but public interest demands that data—especially when it affects health, safety, or knowledge—be shared responsibly. The challenge is balancing respect for participants and institutional rights with the ethical duty to maximize social benefit.
---

Give me your critical thoughts on the following essay:
# Can AI Personalize Ethics?
## From Fixed Rules to Flexible Moral Reasoning
Most ethical systems today still assume that moral rules must apply universally, regardless of who we are, where we live, or what we face. Kantian ethics, for instance, insists on absolute moral duties: rules that must be followed in all situations, without exception. But that assumption ignores how people actually reason through moral problems. My claim is this:
Ethics should not be treated as a fixed system of universal rules, but as a flexible practice of reasoning that adapts to individual circumstances, values, and cultural contexts.
Why? Because moral life is not lived in abstraction. We make ethical decisions not by following formulas, but by weighing reasons, anticipating consequences, and defending our choices. In this light, Stephen Toulmin’s model of reasoning becomes useful; not because it gives us moral answers, but because it explains how people justify those answers in practice. Toulmin shows that arguments are structured by claims, reasons, warrants, and conditions—and that all of these depend on the situation. Ethics works the same way. What we call “right” or “wrong” often rests not on fixed logic, but on reasoning that is responsive to context.
This is already how much of our digital world operates. Medical treatments are personalized to a patient’s genome. Advertisements are tailored to browsing history. Legal decisions are increasingly informed by algorithms that adjust to risk profiles. Yet ethics, the system that governs what we ought to do, still clings to one-size-fits-all formulas.
But this view is not new. In Hindu ethics, for example, moral reasoning is often contextual, balancing competing values like satya (truth) and dharma (duty). One of the most famous illustrations of this comes from the Mahābhārata.
In the Mahābhārata, during the final stages of the Kurukshetra war, Krishna advises Yudhishthira to announce the death of Ashwatthama to demoralize Drona. Yudhishthira complies, declaring, "Ashwatthama is dead," but adds—barely audibly—that it was the elephant, not the warrior. Though technically not a lie, this half-truth illustrates the moral tension between satya and dharma. Krishna defends the act as necessary to serve a higher moral purpose: ending a brutal war and restoring cosmic order.
This moment captures a key idea at the heart of contextual ethics: that what is right cannot always be determined by abstract rules alone. Moral judgment, in this tradition, involves reasoning through the complexity of the situation—not simply following pre-set principles. This kind of reasoning—situational, justificatory, and open to interpretation—offers a compelling alternative to rigid moral universals, especially in an age where artificial intelligence, personalized systems, and global moral diversity are reshaping how we think about responsibility and choice.
Still, no argument for contextual or personalized ethics can be complete without addressing the concerns it raises. From the fear of relativism to the risks of algorithmic bias, critics pose serious questions that deserve thoughtful replies.
Critics claim that personalized ethics threaten fairness, encourage relativism, or hand too much power to flawed technologies. But these concerns often rest on an assumption that universal rules are inherently just. That assumption fails to consider how rigid frameworks can erase difference, ignore social context, and reinforce inequality. A person-centered approach to ethics does not mean moral chaos; it means responding to complexity with judgment rather than applying rules mechanically. In fact, we already personalize moral reasoning in fields like law, medicine, and education—where context matters, lives differ, and judgment is essential. With safeguards like transparency, public reasoning, and accountability, personalized ethics can often serve fairness better than one-size-fits-all rules. And while AI cannot understand context as humans do, it can still assist us—not by replacing moral thinking, but by amplifying it: surfacing relevant values, reducing bias, and helping us reason more clearly in difficult cases.
In an age defined by personalization—from targeted ads to individualized medicine—our ethical frameworks cannot remain fixed and inflexible. The story of Yudhishthira and Ashwatthama reminds us that truth and duty often pull in different directions, and that moral clarity frequently demands more than abstract rules—it requires judgment. As artificial intelligence increasingly mediates our decisions, we have an opportunity not to mechanize morality, but to deepen it. By recognizing that ethics is fundamentally a practice of situated reasoning—grounded in human lives, cultural contexts, and evolving technologies—we can move toward a more responsive, inclusive, and ultimately just moral landscape.

## Further Reading

Sen, A. (2009). The idea of justice. Harvard University Press.

[Framework]
3.4 Analytical Framework This study adopts a dual analytical framework that combines Halliday’s transitivity system (2014) with van Leeuwen’s socio-semantic model of social actor representation (2008). Together, these frameworks allow for a systematic investigation of how actions, events, and participants are linguistically constructed in news discourse, and how social actors are positioned ideologically within narratives of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. 3.4.1 Halliday’s Transitivity System Halliday’s Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) provides a framework for understanding how language encodes experience through the transitivity system. Each clause represents a process, its participants, and related circumstances. Transitivity distinguishes six main types of processes, each shaping discourse in distinct ways: Material Processes (doing/happening) – Represent physical actions and events. Participants include the Actor (doer) and Goal (affected). For example: The army launched an attack. Mental Processes (sensing) – Represent processes of perception, cognition, emotion, and desire. Participants include the Senser (the conscious being) and the Phenomenon (what is sensed). Subtypes include: Cognition (think, know), Perception (see, hear), Affect/Reaction (like, fear, hate). Example: Citizens feared the explosion. Relational Processes (being/having) – Represent states of being, identity, and possession. They may take an attributive form (Carrier–Attribute) or identifying form (Identified–Identifier). Example: The ceasefire was fragile. Verbal Processes (saying) – Represent acts of speech, reporting, or quoting. Participants include the Sayer, Receiver, Verbiage, and sometimes a Target. Example: The minister said peace was possible. Behavioral Processes (behaving) – Represent physiological and psychological behaviors, situated between material and mental processes. The participant is the Behaver, as in The crowd watched in silence. Existential Processes (existing) – Represent the existence of entities or events, often realized by there + be. The participant is the Existent. Example: There was an explosion in the city. In news discourse, these processes are not neutral: Material processes often construct agency and responsibility for violent acts. Mental processes reveal perceptions and ideological stances. Relational processes define identities and roles. Verbal processes manage sources, voices, and credibility. Behavioral processes dramatize reactions and observations. Existential processes present events as unquestionable realities. 3.4.2 van Leeuwen’s Socio-Semantic Model While Halliday’s framework focuses on clause-level grammatical choices, van Leeuwen’s (2008) socio-semantic model examines the broader representational strategies used to position social actors in discourse. This model identifies how actors are included, excluded, categorized, and associated in ways that construct ideology. The main categories are: Exclusion – Social actors may be omitted entirely (suppression) or mentioned elsewhere but not linked to specific actions (backgrounding). Exclusions may be incidental or systematically ideological. Role Allocation – Actors can be represented as active agents (activation) or as passive recipients (passivation). Passivation may occur as subjection (being acted upon) or beneficialisation (benefiting from actions). Generic and Specific Reference – Actors may be represented generically (e.g., “immigrants”) or specifically (e.g., “Benjamin Netanyahu”). Generic reference often establishes “us” and “them” distinctions. Assimilation – Actors may be represented as part of a group (collectivisation) or quantified statistically (aggregation), sometimes reducing individuality. Association and Dissociation – Actors may be linked with others to imply unity or shared responsibility (association) or separated to highlight contrast (dissociation). Indetermination and Differentiation – Indetermination represents actors vaguely or anonymously (e.g., “someone said”), while differentiation emphasizes contrast between groups (e.g., “uptown” vs. “downtown” people). Nomination and Categorisation – Actors may be named (nomination) or described by category (categorisation). Nomination may be formal, semi-formal, or informal. Categorisation has several subtypes: Functionalisation: defined by roles or activities (e.g., “soldiers,” “teachers”). Identification: defined by attributes such as gender, ethnicity, kinship, or class. Subtypes include: Classification (age, gender, race, etc.), Relational identification (roles such as “mother,” “colleague”), Physical identification (appearance, e.g., “the blonde woman”). Appraisement: actors defined by evaluative labels (e.g., “victim,” “terrorist”). Personalisation and Impersonalisation – Actors may be represented as humans (personalisation) or through abstractions, institutions, or objects (impersonalisation). Impersonalisation can occur via: Objectivation (place, instrument, utterance, body part), Abstraction (qualities, e.g., “problems,” “threats”). Overdetermination – Actors may be assigned multiple roles or identities simultaneously, often used to emphasise complexity or to navigate politically sensitive contexts. This framework highlights how language systematically shapes perceptions of identity, agency, and responsibility. 3.4.3 Integrating Transitivity and Social Actor Analysis By combining Halliday’s transitivity system and van Leeuwen’s socio-semantic model, this study examines not only what processes are used to represent events but also how social actors are positioned in relation to those processes. For example, material processes can be analysed alongside role allocation (activation/passivation) to determine whether Palestinians and Israelis are portrayed as agents of violence, as victims, or as absent altogether. Similarly, relational processes can be linked to categorisation strategies to explore how identities are defined in terms of ethnicity, function, or evaluation.
